newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Soft imports keep Australian rate cut on agenda.
newsitem.headline: Soft imports keep Australian rate cut on agenda.

text.p: A small rise in Australia's imports bill for August points to underlying softness in the economy that leaves the door open for another cut in interest rates this year, economists said on Wednesday.

Merchandise imports rose by 1.1 percent in the month, official figures showed, but the rise was due to the inclusion of a A$96 million (US$75.6 million) aircraft and followed three consecutive falls in the monthly data. Without the aircraft, imports would have fallen again, economists said.

"The big story for us is that imports remain soft. It's a reflection of a soft economy, and we think the Reserve Bank will have to move on monetary policy before Christmas just to get the place going again," State Bank of New South Wales chief economist Hans Kunnen told Reuters.

Whether the Reserve Bank of Australia will cut rates again has been the prime concern of markets since it cut its key rate by 0.5 percentage points to 7.0 percent on July 31 -- the first Australian interest rate cut in three years.
Imports are one measure of demand, and so economists said the signs of continuing weakness in the series suggested that that the economy remained soft.

"The fact that imports rose only slightly -- indeed would have fallen again but for a plane -- after three successive falls confirms our view that imports are clearly currently soft, consistent with softness in overall demand," Bankers Trust Australia chief economist Chris Caton said.
As a result, the data helped fuel the sentiment favouring another rate cut before the end of the year.

"It still leaves the door open for another cut in interest rates if the economy's growth rate continues to run below potential between now and the end of the year, which is what these numbers today tend to suggest," ANZ Bank senior Treasury economist David de Garis said.
Within the total rise in imports, consumption goods were up 7.9 percent, capital goods rose 4.3 percent, while intermediate goods fell 4.0 percent.
Economists were most concerned about the weakness seen in capital goods.
While the inclusion of the aircraft saw them rise in the month, capital goods -- goods used for production -- have fallen more than 18 percent in the past three months.
"Of greatest concern is the weakness in imports of capital goods," said Nomura Research senior economist Andrew Pease.
The government has forecast business investment to rise by 14 percent in the fiscal year to June 30, 1997.
While investment intentions surveys suggest that the forecast is on target, capital goods imports are also seen as an indicator of business investment.

The investment forecast is seen as underpinning the government's 3.5 percent economic growth forecast, so signs of weakness would buoy expectations of a rate cut by raising doubts about the growth forecast, economists said.
"There will need to be a substantial rebound in capital goods imports if the government's budget forecast is to be met," Pease said.

After the imports figures were released, economists' initial forecasts for the August current account deficit, to be released on September 30, ranged from A$1.2 billion to A$1.5 billion, continuing the recent run of market-tolerable deficits.
